The site might be $200 but isn't hosting expensive?

Image hosting in and of itself as not very complicated and there are free software solutions available, so buying software based on the fact that it looks similar is inadvisable. The important questions for hosting images are things like how are you going to scale storage, do backups, pay for bandwidth, handle attacks, maintain performance, handle legal requests from private individuals, corporations, police, three letter type agencies and governments in general, make enough money off selling advertising targeting uploaders when most of your costs go to hot linked images that don't advertise unless you use annoying water marks, make fixes and modifications, whether to incorporate to avoid liability, and finally, what kind of jazzy user interface or slick looking website you're going to have and what's your web address going to be.

I understand the desire to just jump in and figure it out as you go, but providing a good image hosting service is exponentially more difficult than simply providing an image hosting service. And it's annoying to have services die out. If you really are committed, then I suppose some of the questions could wait to be answered by employees if you could make it profitable enough for employees, but being that profitable would be really difficult. Mostly you need to be able and willing to do it all yourself and if at some point you can afford to offload some of the work, that's great, but don't count on it. So if you're willing and able to do it all yourself, where should you start? My suggestion is to start by learning to program and writing the software yourself. You may need to start over from scratch a few times before you've figured out a minimally acceptable design, and possible more times later which will be complicated a bit by having a shitload of data that needs to be ported over, but it's doable. Formal education and work experience is very handy, but not strictly required. I personally like the Go programming language. It has a medium difficult learning curve, but it'll pay dividends later on in the process. The Python programming language has an easier initial learning curve and technically could work once the app is large scale, but the bigger you get, the more burdensome it will become, and starting over in a different language once you've got something big, is a pain in the ass.
